extracted.intended_audience: empirical researchers, policy analysts, and economists studying patent examination processes and examiner behavior
extracted.subtask_short: empirical analysis of patent examiner behavior
extracted.subtask_description: Quantitative evaluation of how patent examiner grade-level promotions and years of experience affect application outcomes (grant rates, rejection types, citation patterns) using PAIR data and fixed-effects regressions. Emphasis on identification strategies, robustness checks, and interpretation of mechanisms (time constraints vs scrutiny/shirking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate grade-level promotion effects from experience effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential to our analysis is the separation of the effects stemming from grade-level promotions and from the acquisition of additional years of experience within the Agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify these forces by exploiting that promotions and experience do not perfectly correlate; include year fixed effects and examiner fixed effects to identify GS-level changes while capturing experience movements in year increments. Use additional specifications (experience dummies in two-year blocks, nesting experience years within grade levels) to further decouple promotion from experience effects. Acknowledge limitations where year and experience cannot be separately identified without extra normalization restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examiner and year fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Regressions include examiner and year fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner fixed effects control for time-invariant heterogeneity across examiners; year fixed effects capture common time trends. Note: including examiner and year fixed effects can subsume experience effects unless additional normalization (e.g., experience dummies) is imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster standard errors at the examiner level
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard errors are clustered at the examiner level to correct for autocorrelation within given examiners over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report clustered standard errors (in parentheses) and significance levels (* 10%, ** 5%, *** 1%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regress granted incidence on GS-level dummy variables (omit reference group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regress the incidence of an application being granted on a set of dummy variables capturing each of the relevant examiner pay grades (GS-7 through GS-14), with the dummy for GS-7 omitted as the reference group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both GS-13 without and with partial signatory authority as separate dummies. Present coefficients with confidence intervals (figures) and tabular regression results (tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experience dummies in two-year blocks to isolate experience effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify examiner experience dummies into two-year blocks—i.e., 0-1 years, 2-3 years, 4-5 years, etc.—to attempt separate estimation of GS-level, year and experience effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach allows presentation of experience-group coefficients while leaving year effects as nuisance controls; plot experience-group coefficients to visualize inverse-U patterns in grant rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nest experience years within grade levels (within-grade experience effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate specifications that include dummy variables capturing specific years within specific grade levels (e.g., 0-1 years in GS-13, 2-3 years in GS-13, 0-1 years in GS-14, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on GS-12 and above where more examiners spend multiple years; track examiners across 2-year increments within each grade to visualize independent and discontinuous impacts of promotions and within-grade tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced-sample robustness: follow examiners who experience all indicated promotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Create balanced-sample analogs that follow more select groups of examiners who experience each of the indicated promotions (e.g., started GS-7 and ascended to at least GS-14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use balanced-sample specifications (Columns 5 and 6 / Online Appendix exercises) to confirm robustness of estimated GS-level effects against sample imbalance concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for application covariates (entity size, prosecution duration, duration squared)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include controls for the entity size status of the applicant (large or small entity) and for the duration (in days) between filing and final disposition of the application, along with the square of this duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding these covariates should not materially change the GS-level coefficient pattern (Column 3 evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include technology-by-year fixed effects to rule out technology-switching confounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Include technology-by-year fixed effects to rule out concerns that the results may reflect examiners switching to different technologies as they are promoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This control addresses potential confounding from changing economic/technology environments; results remain virtually unchanged with these fixed effects (Column 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for incidence of Request-for-Continued Examination (RCE) or restrict to no-RCE subsample
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a control for the incidence of an RCE associated with the application, and alternatively condition the analysis on applications without an RCE filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because RCEs prolong examination and may affect allowance probabilities, controlling for RCEs helps ensure promotion/experience effects are not driven by continuation dynamics. Results persist with RCE controls (slightly smaller magnitudes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsification test using applicant characteristic examiners cannot change
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct a falsification exercise estimating the relationship between promotions and a characteristic the examiner cannot alter (large vs small-entity applicant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect no systematic change in this variable with promotions; finding no significant change (from GS-12 onwards) lends confidence to random sorting of applications across grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude GS-15 examiners from primary analysis (and test inclusion in robustness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude applications examined by GS-15 examiners from the primary analysis due to discrepancies between official time-allotment schedules and observed time allotments for GS-15 examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude <3% of applications; also run specifications including GS-15 under the official assumption (less time) to check robustness—patterns remain similar (Online Appendix Figures A6/A7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address examination duration imbalance with alternative sampling window
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin observation in 2004 and confine the sample to applications disposed of within a three-year period to ensure consistency in the mix of application prosecution durations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alternative specification addresses the possibility that earlier-year dispositions disproportionately reflect quicker applications; results are robust to this sampling approach (Online Appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure obviousness rejection effort via a relative share metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the dependent variable for obviousness effort as the ratio of obviousness rejections to the sum of rejections across: obviousness, lack of novelty, lack of patentable subject matter/utility, and failure to satisfy disclosure requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the data cannot capture the full force of any given obviousness rejection (number of claims affected, ease of overcoming), the relative-share measure provides a proxy for the relative effort devoted to time-intensive obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple outcome measures beyond grant rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze relationships between examiner GS-levels and various application/patent outcomes: share of rejections based on obviousness, share of prior-art citations from examiner, incidence of renewal at 4 and 8 years, forward-looking citations (logged), generality score (logged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run separate regressions for each outcome (see Table 4 columns) and interpret patterns jointly to infer mechanisms (e.g., falling obviousness shares suggest reduced time-intensive analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source and sample definition: PAIR data, final dispositions between March 2001 and July 2012
rubrics_metrics.description: Each observation is a given application from the PAIR database that reached a final disposition and that was published in the PAIR records between March 2001 and July 2012.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sample sizes (N) for each specification; be explicit about time window, inclusion/exclusion criteria and subsamples used for particular outcomes (e.g., only applications culminating in issuance for citation-based outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Present estimated coefficients with confidence intervals in figures and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures plot estimated coefficients (means) with 95% confidence intervals (vertical bars). Tables report coefficients with clustered standard errors in parentheses and significance stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit CIs in some figures for visual clarity when noted; always make clear omitted/reference groups for interpretation (e.g., GS-7 omitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate omitted/reference groups for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit baseline categories like GS-7 for GS-level regressions and 0-1 years for experience-group regressions so coefficients represent changes relative to those references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state omitted groups in notes and ensure figures/tables reflect that baseline for relative grant/rjection rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about identification limitations and rely on robustness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that specifications with examiner fixed effects and year effects cannot always distinguish year and experience effects without normalization; discuss selection/retention concerns (quick risers vs slow risers) and limits of generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use balanced samples, falsification tests, alternative specifications, and nested-experience approaches to mitigate and probe these limitations; interpret local findings conservatively where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret promotion-induced changes with alternative mechanism explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider multiple theories for observed behavior changes upon promotion—(a) reduced time allotted to examiners following promotions leading to less scrutiny of patentability, (b) increased informal shirking or reduced supervisory scrutiny as examiners are promoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mechanisms empirically by comparing patterns across rejection bases (obviousness most time-intensive shows largest decline), by considering promotions that do not carry formal authority changes, and by examining within-grade temporal dynamics (immediate jump upon promotion followed by decline over years is more consistent with time-constraint story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge data limitations on rejection intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: The data capture the incidence of any obviousness rejection but do not reveal the full force (e.g., whether it covers one claim or many, how easy it is to overcome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relative-share measures and multiple robustness checks rather than relying on raw counts; explicitly note the limitation when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track within-grade temporal patterns to infer learning vs promotion effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot grant rates and obviousness rejection shares as examiners increase tenure within specific grade levels to observe inverse-U or decline patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If grant rates jump upon entering a grade then fall over years at that grade, interpret this as promotion-induced time-allotment changes interrupting learning; use these within-grade trajectories as evidence against simple monotonic experience effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use falsification and multiple robustness checks to bolster causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ falsification exercises (e.g., large-entity status), balanced-sample analyses, controls for RCEs, alternative sample windows, technology-by-year fixed effects, and inclusion/exclusion of GS-15 examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whether patterns persist across these checks; use them to build confidence in causal interpretation while transparently reporting remaining caveats.
